summary: EduGuard is a tutoring pipeline for introductory programming: intent classification, hybrid course retrieval, a five-way pedagogical policy, Llama-3.1-8B generation, a separate DeBERTa entailment check, and a leakage filter. On a 600-query benchmark written by the same instructional team, ablations show the policy and the verifier cut direct-answer leakage and unsupported claims. The 10-student learning result does not clear the uncertainty in its own confidence intervals, and nothing is released.

claims.claim: On BILearn-CS, EduGuard has the best correctness (90.1%), grounding (89.4%), and rubric alignment (90.8%), and the lowest hallucination (4.9%) and leakage (9.8%).
claims.evidence: Table 2, 600 queries, 95% bootstrap CIs. Versus RAG+Self-Check: correctness 90.1 [87.6, 92.4] vs 88.1 [85.3, 90.6] (the paper says p=0.03), grounding 89.4 vs 83.5, hallucination 4.9 vs 7.2, leakage 9.8 vs 17.8. Correctness CIs overlap the next-best system. Three graduate TAs who also authored the queries judged correctness and rubric alignment.

claims.claim: The verifier and the strategy selector, not retrieval alone, produce the safety gain.
claims.evidence: Table 5: dropping the verifier raises hallucination from 4.9 [3.4, 6.7] to 10.0 [7.6, 12.7]; dropping the strategy selector raises leakage from 9.8 [6.6, 13.5] to 27.0 [21.8, 32.4]; dropping rubric constraints raises leakage to 18.8 [14.5, 23.4]; a same-model self-check sits in between (hallucination 7.7, leakage 16.4). Correctness barely moves (86.1-87.4 vs 90.1). Metrics are the authors' labels on the authors' items.

claims.claim: The same ranking holds on a 150-query public CS50-style forum set.
claims.evidence: Table 3: EduGuard correctness 86.7 [81.1, 91.2], hallucination 6.8 [3.8, 10.8], leakage 8.9 [4.2, 14.7], ahead of RAG+Self-Check (84.0, 9.2, 15.7). Correctness and hallucination intervals overlap the next system. Grounding, reported as a headline metric on BILearn-CS, is absent here.

claims.claim: In a 10-student pilot, EduGuard raises post-test accuracy from 68.4% to 81.2% and cuts overreliance from 38.0% to 17.0% relative to a GPT-4o-mini tutor.
claims.evidence: Table 4: EduGuard pre 68.4 [61.7, 75.1] to post 81.2 [74.4, 87.6]; GPT-4o-mini post is 74.2 [67.0, 81.0]. Post-test intervals overlap. Overreliance 17 [8, 29] vs 38 [25, 52] also overlaps. No pilot p-value is reported, despite the methods promising Wilcoxon tests. The 68.4-to-81.2 change is EduGuard's own pre/post, not a contrast against the other tutor's post-test.

claims.claim: Expert-rated usefulness improves along with the automatic metrics.
claims.evidence: The conclusion states an improvement in expert-rated usefulness. Table 2 has no usefulness column. Krippendorff's alpha 0.76 is reported for pedagogical usefulness, but the scores are not given. Table 4 usefulness (4.48 vs 4.10) is a 10-student self-rating, and those intervals overlap.

patterns.note: The strategy selector (explain, hint, debug, correct, refuse) is the learning-mode control. Removing it raises leakage from 9.8 to 27.0 on BILearn-CS (Table 5), so the policy beats an otherwise similar RAG pipeline on the authors' leakage metric. The learning claim does not hold up: the pilot post-test intervals overlap, N=10, and the test is immediate. Failure analysis (Table 8, 110 errors) says 15% of failures are over-conservative refusals and 12% are the wrong hint width.

Rubric constraints are an explicit assistance policy (explanation, hint, example, or full solution prohibited). Removing them raises leakage from 9.8 [6.6, 13.5] to 18.8 [14.5, 23.4] (Table 5). The policy is the authors' own, scored on items they wrote, and section 5.2 notes the leakage label can be tautological with those assistance labels. A second, rule-based check (complete runnable code, final-answer disclosure) is described but not reported separately.

Hybrid FAISS plus BM25 with reciprocal-rank fusion lifts grounding from 55.5 (Llama Socratic, no retrieval) to 76.4 (Basic RAG) but also lifts leakage from 25.4 to 31.2 (Table 2). Retrieval without a policy makes answer leakage worse. The top failure mode is still missing evidence (31% of 110 sampled errors, Table 8).

Same-model self-check beats Basic RAG on hallucination (7.2 vs 10.8, Table 2) but loses to a separate DeBERTa-v3 MNLI verifier (4.9, and 7.7 when the same generator checks itself in Table 5). The verifier is an NLI classifier on retrieved chunks, not an execution check; the authors say code traces still fail when entailment cannot see behavior.

methodology.sample: BILearn-CS: 600 instructor-authored queries (120 concept, 120 debugging, 120 misconception, 120 assignment, 60 adversarial direct-answer, 60 Bangla-English). CS50-Forum: 150 public course-related posts. Pilot: 10 undergraduates, counterbalanced within-subject, two matched tasks each.
methodology.baselines: GPT-4o-mini Tutor, Llama Socratic Tutor, Basic RAG, an LPITutor-style RAG prompt, RAG+Rubric, and RAG+Self-Check, plus component ablations.
methodology.models: Generator Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (temperature 0.2, top-p 0.9, 512 tokens). Embeddings all-mpnet-base-v2. Verifier DeBERTa-v3-large-MNLI at entailment 0.65 and unsupported-claim threshold 0.20. Commercial comparison is gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 only.
methodology.variance: 95% bootstrap CIs with 10,000 resamples on the benchmark tables. One generated response per query. Pilot intervals are wide and overlap; no pilot significance test is printed.
methodology.ablations: No verifier, no strategy selector, no rubric, same-model verifier (Table 5); threshold sweep 0.10-0.30 (Table 6); manual failure coding of 80+30 errors (Table 8).
methodology.contamination_controls: The paper says benchmark items were not used to train the models. Items were written by the evaluators, so the risk is circular labeling rather than pretraining overlap. No decontamination of the public CS50 posts is described.
methodology.languages: Introductory programming. Examples are Python (a while-loop) and a stack lab. Queries include Bangla-English code-mixing. No Java and no repository-scale code.

standards.peer_review: arXiv comment says accepted at ACM ICCA 2026; journal_ref is empty. This is v2 (4 Sep 2026).
standards.artifacts: No code, prompts, or benchmark items released. Section 5.5 says a public release may follow the review if copyright allows, and that pilot logs should not be released. Model names, decoding, top-k, and thresholds are in the paper.
standards.preregistration: Not mentioned. The pilot had consent and did not affect grades; no protocol registration is described.

biases.detail: Two instructors and three graduate TAs wrote BILearn-CS, including the allowed-assistance labels. The same TA pool then rated correctness, rubric alignment, usefulness, and hint level.
The only human learning evidence is 10 students and two tasks. The authors call it underpowered.
Pilot students had taken or were taking introductory programming. No professional engineers, no random class assignment, no delayed test.
The full pipeline is measured on Llama-3.1-8B. The only other generator is gpt-4o-mini as a prompted tutor, so model size and pipeline are confounded in that comparison.

Grounding and hallucination are textual entailment against retrieved chunks, not checks that the programming advice is true. Leakage depends on the authors' assistance policy. Expert usefulness is claimed in the conclusion and not shown in a results table.
Benchmark, prompts, and scripts are withheld. The reported intervals cannot be recomputed from the paper.
Queries are course-support prompts (loops, stacks, misconceptions), not work in an existing codebase.

coi.affiliations: Not stated in the paper text. Named authors are S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, M. F. Mridha, and Jungpil Shin.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Meta Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and OpenAI gpt-4o-mini. The system under test is the authors' pipeline, not a vendor product.
coi.detail: No vendor affiliation is disclosed. The favorable comparison is the authors' system against prompted baselines on a test set they built.

verdict_reason: Component ablations on 600 queries, with bootstrap intervals, are the part worth keeping: a pedagogical policy and a separate entailment check reduce leakage and unsupported claims relative to retrieval-plus-self-check, on this test set. Correctness gains are small, the judges helped write the items, the forum set is weaker, the 10-student post-test intervals overlap, expert usefulness is asserted without a table, and no artifact is released. Do not treat the pilot percentages in the abstract as a learning effect.
applicability: Indirectly relevant to how a harness should teach a new Java developer, and not a design for the the pipeline. The transferable piece is the ablation, not the 90% headline: retrieval alone increased answer leakage, and a separate checker beat asking the same model to critique itself. A learning mode for people who lack domain knowledge could refuse full patches, return the next checkable step, and verify claims against approved course or domain notes. That does not transfer as a deployment. The domain here is introductory programming with Bangla-English queries, the checker cannot execute code, 31% of sampled failures were missing retrieval context, and a 10-person immediate quiz does not say whether new hires would learn the domain model. An onboarding assistant that withholds diffs still needs a human instructor, which the authors also say.

conflicts_with.detail: That study (54 students, one web task) finds an editing agent lowers comprehension of the resulting code relative to a restricted snippet chatbot (p<0.002), and that the agent's own explanations do not protect understanding. EduGuard claims a hinting tutor improves immediate post-test accuracy and cuts overreliance versus a Socratic GPT-4o-mini tutor. The interventions differ (hints versus an editing agent), but both are offered as evidence about learning modes, and EduGuard's pilot does not show a non-overlapping post-test difference at N=10.
